Does Google Sheets have a way to sort by more than one column at once?

Short answer: Yes, on the web, through one specific dialog. Highlight the cells, then Data > Sort range > Advanced range sorting options, choose the first column and its direction, and click Add another sort column for each further level. That dialog is the only documented multi-column sort in the interface — the right-click commands on a column letter sort by one column only, and the Android and iPhone apps document nothing beyond a single key.
Does Google Sheets have a way to sort by more than one column at once?

The distinction that decides the answer is range versus sheet, not column count. Google documents two separate sort commands with different scopes, and only the range command opens a dialog that stacks sort keys. Someone who reaches for sorting by right-clicking a column heading — the faster and more discoverable route — never sees the multi-column option and can reasonably conclude it does not exist.

Each rule after the first is a tie-breaker within the rules above it, which is what "sort by more than one column at once" normally means.

Verified — SORT is documented as multi-column in its first sentence. SORT function: "Sorts the rows of a given array or range by the values in one or more columns." Its signature is SORT(range, sort_column, is_ascending, [sort_column2, is_ascending2, ...]), and the trailing optional pairs are "Additional columns and sort order flags beyond the first, in order of precedence."

Verified — SORTN adds a row limit to the same multi-key sort. SORTN "Returns the first n items in a data set after performing a sort," with signature SORTN(range, [n], [display_ties_mode], [sort_column1, is_ascending1], ...). Its later pairs are "Additional columns and sort order flags used if a tie happens, in order of precedence" — the same precedence model, described from the tie-breaking side.

Is there a way to download an image out of a Google Sheet?

Short answer: For two of the three ways an image can sit in a spreadsheet, yes. For the third — an image floating over the cells, which is what you get by dragging a picture in — Google documents no download path at all: none in the interface, none in Apps Script, none in the Sheets API, and no download format that produces the image as its own file. An image placed in a cell has exactly one documented route, the Apps Script call CellImage.getContentUrl(), which returns a short-lived Google-hosted URL. An image placed by the IMAGE() function needs no extraction, because the cell's formula already holds the source URL.
Is there a way to download an image out of a Google Sheet?

The answer splits three ways because "an image in a sheet" names three different objects. Google's own insert flow offers the choice and then documents the three results separately, with different menus, different Apps Script classes, and different amounts of documentation. Right-clicking the picture and hunting for a save command is the natural first attempt, and it lands on the one variant Google documents nothing for.

Grafana is an open-source, interactive data visualization and monitoring platform that allows users to query, visualize, and understand data from various sources, creating dashboards for easier interpretation and collaboration.
A graph database stores data as nodes and relationships (edges), with properties on both, so the primary question is what connects to what rather than which row matches this key.
It matters when the interesting fact is the link: a knowledge garden's wikilinks, a social graph, a bill of materials, or a fraud ring are cheaper to traverse as edges than to reconstruct with joins.
Contrasts with a table store (rows and foreign keys) and with a document store (nested trees). A graph engine treats adjacency as a first-class index.
This garden already uses the metaphor: journaling is Chron/ological/Order; knowledge gardening clusters related pages the way a graph clusters neighbors — what goes where more than what happened.
Nodes and relationships are data — the edge is not an afterthought join; it has a type and can carry properties.
Local traversal — queries walk neighborhoods (friends-of-friends, citation chains) without scanning the whole store.
Index-free adjacency (ideal) — each node knows its neighbors directly; cost grows with the walk, not with table size.
Two common models: labeled-property graphs (nodes/edges with labels and maps of properties) and RDF triples (subject–predicate–object).
Query languages include Cypher / GQL, Gremlin, SPARQL, and vendor languages such as AQL.
Neo4j — native property graph; Cypher; the engine most cited in this garden.
Amazon Neptune — managed graph on AWS (property graph and RDF).
JanusGraph — distributed open-source graph over Cassandra/HBase, queried with Gremlin.
"A graph database is a knowledge graph" — False; a knowledge graph is a modeled web of meaning; a graph database is one way to store it.
"Graphs replace SQL" — Oversimplified; they win on relationship-heavy queries and lose on simple tabular aggregates unless the product is multi-model.
